Before you begin

Work individually, with nearby discussion if useful. Predict before each comparison. No R or GLM experience is required. You may run the supplied code or read the figures and result sheet; both routes answer the same questions.

Use the prepared browser R environment. If access fails, open this HTML and the result sheet locally and answer the same questions. There is one core exercise today. Demonstrations and optional extensions are labelled. No installation, independent Stan programming or homework is required.

Core exercise: which mother-tree estimates will move?

Purpose Explain information sharing using each mother tree’s data and the model’s assumptions.
Computation Supplied partial-pooling fit plus exact Beta updating for the two comparison models. No new Stan inference.
Data Eight mother trees of one species. Simulated, and different from the Day 2 quadrats.

This example leaves out the density predictor so that we can focus on differences among mother trees. The binomial survival model is shared with Days 1 and 2. Mother trees and species are different kinds of groups.

1. Predict before seeing the fitted results

trees <- make_tree_data()
trees |>
  select(tree, n, suv) |>
  mutate(observed_proportion = suv / n)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#>   tree      n   suv observed_proportion
#>   <chr> <int> <int>               <dbl>
#> 1 A        15     6              0.4
#> 2 B        39    18              0.462
#> 3 C        24     6              0.25
#> 4 D        50    19              0.38
#> 5 E        32     6              0.188
#> 6 F        38    12              0.316
#> 7 G        21     1              0.0476
#> 8 H        50    12              0.24

Choose two trees whose estimates you expect to change when they share information. Write their letters and your reasons. Consider both seedling count and the observed survival proportion.

2. Compare three ways of estimating survival

  • Complete pooling assumes one shared survival probability.
  • Separate estimates give each mother tree an independent probability.
  • Partial pooling gives trees their own probabilities and estimates a shared distribution.
fit <- course_fit("day3_trees")
fit$source
#> [1] "precomputed"
comparison <- mother_comparison(fit, seed = 20261024)
plot_mother_comparison(comparison)
plot_mother_truth(comparison, trees)

Purple open points show separate estimates; orange filled points show partial pooling. The grey vertical line shows the complete-pooling posterior mean, and the grey ribbon shows its 95% credible interval. Coloured bars are also 95% credible intervals. Rows are ordered by the separate posterior means, and n is the seedling count. Separate and partial intervals are offset vertically within each tree to keep them distinct. The grey line is a comparison reference, not the exact target of hierarchical shrinkage.

The second plot compares estimates (y) with the generating probabilities (x). The dashed diagonal marks equality with the truth. Vertical connections show movement from Separate to Partial pooling. Tree H (n = 50) changes only slightly, towards its generating probability of 0.29. Not every tree moves closer to the truth; in real data, the truth is unknown.

The complete and separate models use the Day 1 flat Beta(1,1) prior on each probability. The partial model uses Normal group effects on the logit scale, with their centre and SD estimated from all trees. Thus the prior specifications also differ across these comparisons.

3. Interpret the movement

Did your predictions agree with the figures? Explain one tree’s change in words. Would information sharing have the same strength if the data supported large differences among mother trees? Give a reason.

TipSolution and instructor notes

The largest movement in this data set is tree G, with 21 seedlings. Its separate posterior mean is 0.09 and its partial-pooling mean is 0.17. Ask participants to connect the movement to both sample size and position relative to the inferred group distribution.

Less information within a group often gives the shared distribution more influence. Greater inferred between-group variation generally weakens sharing. It does not move every estimate by a fixed amount or guarantee improvement for every tree. The target is an inferred distribution on the logit scale, not mechanically the pooled observed proportion. The comparison also changes the prior formulation.

The true rates are known only because the data are simulated. If revealing them, use trees$p_true. Similar true rates make complete pooling competitive here. This does not make exact equality a justified assumption for all ecological data.

Instructor demonstrations

Shared information as a hierarchical prior

s_j \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,p_j), \qquad \operatorname{logit}(p_j) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma).

Here j indexes mother trees and \sigma is a standard deviation on the logit scale. The supplied stan/logistic.stan uses \mu\sim\mathcal{N}(0,5) and \sigma\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(0,1). All Normal second arguments are SDs.

plot_group_spread()

The centre is fixed in this illustration. Only the group SD changes. These are hypothetical probabilities, not posterior estimates for our eight trees.

NoteCompleted Stan model 
data {
  int<lower=1> I; // number of species
  array[I] int<lower=0> suv; // number of survivors
  array[I] int<lower=0> N; // number of individuals
  array[I] int<lower=1, upper=I> ii; // integer
}

parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  vector[I] z_tilde;
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[I] z;
  z = mu + sigma * z_tilde;
}

model {
  mu ~ normal(0, 5);
  z_tilde ~ std_normal();
  sigma ~ std_normal();
  for (i in 1:I)
    suv[i] ~ binomial_logit(N[i], z[ii[i]]);
}

generated quantities {
  vector[I] log_lik;
  vector[I] p = inv_logit(z);
  for (i in 1:I)
    log_lik[i] = binomial_logit_lpmf(suv[i] | N[i], z[ii[i]]);
}

Computation and ecological checking

course_diagnostics(fit)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   max_rhat min_bulk_ess min_tail_ess divergent max_treedepth min_ebfmi
#>      <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>     <dbl>         <int>     <dbl>
#> 1     1.00         780.        1079.         0             0      0.66
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(fit$draws, pars = c("mu", "sigma"))
plot_mother_check(fit)

Do the sampler diagnostics agree? Does the model reproduce the observed counts by mother tree? Is sharing information among these trees ecologically plausible? A good answer considers all three questions.

Species differences in CNDD

plot_cndd_species()
plot_cndd_abundance()

These are conceptual simulations from the example in main.qmd, not fitted research results. The individual-level question is survival versus conspecific density. The group-level question is whether density coefficients vary with species abundance. The full research analysis is an instructor explanation. A negative coefficient means declining survival on the probability scale. More negative logit coefficients do not imply a fixed probability drop at every baseline.

Another research example: allometry and wood density

The individual-level relationship is height versus DBH. The group-level question is whether species’ allometric exponents vary with wood density. The observation model changes from binomial survival to Normal log height. Information sharing among groups is the common structure.

plot_wood_density()

This figure uses the existing saved fit to simulated tree data. It illustrates interpretation, not an empirical conclusion about wood density in a real forest. No additional participant analysis is required.

Optional extension: a new mother tree

What can we predict about a ninth mother tree before counting its seedlings? Keep the model and fitted data fixed. Add variation among mother trees for each draw.

set.seed(20261026)
draws <- fit$draws
p_new <- plogis(rnorm(nrow(draws), draws$mu, draws$sigma))
course_interval(p_new)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>    mean median  lower upper
#>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 0.293  0.280 0.0765 0.606

Does this describe a survival probability or a future number of survivors?

TipSolution and instructor notes

It describes the survival probability of a new mother tree under the inferred group distribution. It includes uncertainty about the group parameters and variation among mother trees. Predicting a survivor count would also require specifying a seedling count and generating binomial survival.

Connection to your research

Name a grouping in your data and one quantity that may differ among groups. What would justify sharing information? Which predicted pattern would you compare with observations before reporting the result?
